name: Network Isolation Local Execution Test
text:
Offline capability is an architectural test, not a feature label. Kleppmann and coauthors distinguish cloud applications from local-first software by the location of the primary data copy, the presence of a locally installed executable, and continued operation without a network connection. Their prototypes permit users to disconnect, continue working, and later merge changes. Applications centered on synchronous server interaction instead lock users out when the network fails. This independently extends Kaal's operational test: retained function under isolation supplies observable evidence that computation and state remain on the user's device.

The correspondence has limits. Local-first software addresses collaborative data applications, not agent runtimes or model inference. Offline editing does not establish that every relevant computation occurs locally, and later synchronization may still depend on external infrastructure. The paper nevertheless sharpens the classification rule. A local interface cannot establish local execution when the underlying capability disappears at disconnection. Network isolation converts an architectural claim into a falsifiable test.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: “Old-fashioned” apps work fine without an Internet connection, but cloud apps typically don’t work while offline.
Since local-first applications store the primary copy of their data in each device’s local filesystem, the user can read and write this data anytime, even while offline.
Moreover, for good offline support it is desirable for the software to run as a locally installed executable on your device, rather than a tab in a web browser.
Most web apps have little or no support for offline working: if your network hiccups for even a moment, you are locked out of your work mid-sentence
While other applications on the system threw up errors (“offline! warning!”) and blocked the user from working, the local-first prototypes function normally regardless of network status.
Servers thus have a role to play in the local-first world — not as central authorities, but as “cloud peers” that support client applications without being on the critical path.
